Model syllabus

MIND(s): thinking, feeling, and ways of knowing.

A ten-week faculty discussion draft. Seven shared works, supported by short research companions. Designed for three class meetings a week; dates, policies, exact excerpts and common events remain to be agreed.

Go to the weekly sequence

Course description

This course studies minds through scientific explanation, philosophical argument, artistic form and embodied practice. Students examine the relationship between thinking and feeling, the development of skill, the interpretation of experience, and the limits of claims about other minds.

The course begins with a poem and moves among texts, music, art and experiments. Recent research by Michael Levin, Mark Solms and Cameron Berg supplies specific claims to assess alongside competing accounts. Students learn to distinguish a work’s meaning, a theory’s argument and a study’s findings.

Learning outcomes

  • Distinguish cognition, consciousness, attention and affect in a specific source.
  • Summarize a claim accurately and identify its supporting evidence.
  • Analyze a text, musical passage or artwork through details of its form.
  • Compare two disciplinary methods without treating them as equivalent.
  • Develop and revise an argument that addresses a substantive counterargument.

Seven shared works

  1. Blackiston, Dromiack, Grasso and colleagues, including Michael LevinRevealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity
  2. Mark SolmsThe Hard Problem of Consciousness and the Free Energy Principle
  3. Cameron Berg, Diogo de Lucena and Judd RosenblattLarge Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
  4. Zhuangzi; English translation by James LeggeZhuangzi, chapter 3: Nourishing the Lord of Life
  5. Emily DickinsonThe Brain—is wider than the Sky
  6. Steve ReichMusic for 18 Musicians
  7. Lygia ClarkCaminhando (Walking)

Supporting sources appear in the weekly sequence. The linked bank records explain access and evidence limits.

The weekly sequence

Three meetings per week · proposed
Week 1

Naming mind

Starting work: The Brain—is wider than the Sky

  1. Read Dickinson’s complete poem. Introduce working distinctions among mind, brain, cognition, consciousness and affect.
  2. Analyze the poem’s comparisons, syntax and scale.
  3. Compare literary interpretation with a scientific claim.

Writing: Draft a 300-word accurate account of one passage.

Week 2

Feeling and explanation

Starting work: The Hard Problem of Consciousness and the Free Energy Principle

  1. Read Solms’s abstract and introduction; faculty guide the technical vocabulary.
  2. Map an argument from bodily needs to conscious feeling.
  3. Compare supporting observations with theoretical conclusions.

Writing: Submit a 500-word claim-and-evidence summary.

Week 3

Skill and cultivated attention

Starting work: Zhuangzi, chapter 3: Nourishing the Lord of Life

  1. Read chapter 3 in Chinese Text Project’s translation; identify the translator and historical context.
  2. Analyze Cook Ding’s practiced action and moments of caution.
  3. Compare the narrative with the basketball-attention review’s abstract.

Writing: Prepare an evidence table: textual details and empirical measures.

Week 4

Music and shared timing

Starting work: Music for 18 Musicians

  1. Listen to a complete authorized recording of Music for 18 Musicians before class.
  2. Describe two passages using timestamps, pulse, timbre and audible change.
  3. Hold a proposed musician-led session on ensemble coordination.

Writing: Submit a 900-word close analysis of one core work.

Week 5

Art as an encounter

Starting work: Caminhando (Walking)

  1. Read MoMA’s Clark essay, concentrating on Caminhando and its historical setting.
  2. Analyze documentation of the work as object, action and experience.
  3. Compare Clark with the course’s accounts of embodied skill.

Writing: Revise the close analysis after peer and instructor feedback.

Week 6

Coordination across scales

Starting work: Revealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity

  1. Read the author summary, abstract and Figure 1 caption of the tissue study.
  2. Trace the movement from calcium imaging to a network representation.
  3. Compare the finding with Levin and Resnik’s broader theoretical abstract.

Writing: Submit a 1,100-word comparison across two disciplines.

Week 7

Testing an account

Starting work: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness

  1. Read the COGITATE abstract and an instructor-prepared guide to the tested predictions.
  2. Compare predictions, measurements and limitations.
  3. Hold a proposed interdisciplinary panel on evidence and interpretation.

Writing: Submit a final-essay claim with three annotated sources.

Week 8

Artificial minds

Starting work: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing

  1. Read Berg and colleagues’ abstract, then instructor-selected results and limitations.
  2. Compare model self-report with mechanistic evidence.
  3. Read Seth’s abstract as a competing theoretical position.

Writing: Draft a counterargument and identify the evidence needed to assess it.

Week 9

Responsibility under uncertainty

Starting work: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness

  1. Read the introduction or abstract of the Butlin report; faculty select a short indicator passage.
  2. Compare uncertainty about experience with reasons for moral consideration.
  3. Present a five-minute account of an argument using two disciplinary methods.

Writing: Bring a complete final-essay draft for peer review.

Week 10

Making a defensible argument

Starting work: The Brain—is wider than the Sky

  1. Return to the opening poem and revisit the course vocabulary.
  2. Workshop claims, source use and unresolved objections.
  3. Hold a proposed concluding colloquium across sections.

Writing: Submit a 1,600–2,000-word revised essay and a 400-word revision account.

A writing sequence with room to revise

Proposed assessment model, for discussion with the program: the final essay develops from earlier work. These percentages and lengths are draft choices, not current Lawrence policy.

WorkPurposeWeight
Short-writing portfolioAccurate summary, evidence tables and preparatory writing15%
Close analysis + revisionExplain how a core work produces meaning20%
Comparative essayCompare two methods and their limits20%
Final essay + revision accountDefend a claim, use sources and address an objection30%
Preparation, contribution + peer reviewSupport shared inquiry through spoken, written or other agreed accessible contributions15%

Across assignments, assess accuracy, use of specific evidence, quality of reasoning, organization and revision. Students are assessed on their arguments, not agreement with a theory of mind.

Preparing this model for a real class

Reading and teaching support

Use short scientific passages with a glossary and figure guide. The full technical papers belong in faculty preparation and optional extension. Confirm recording access and choose the precise translated editions before setting the common syllabus.

Plan a sustainable workload around the institution’s credit expectations. Pilot the proposed excerpts with first-year readers before fixing page counts. A laboratory or coding background is not a prerequisite for this model.

Access and classroom practice

Provide accessible texts, transcripts and visual descriptions. Offer equivalent ways to complete listening, movement and performance-based work. Personal health history or intimate self-disclosure is never required.

Before adoption, insert the current institutional policies on accommodations, academic integrity, attendance, late work and AI use. Any use of AI in assessed work needs a clear, shared policy and an accurate record of assistance.

Next curriculum review: expand Asian traditions beyond one Chinese text; consider a longer literary work; review global and demographic breadth; test whether the science selections are manageable. This is a concrete starting syllabus, not a completed selection process.
